svg.title: The default OSPF cost formula, why it breaks above one gigabit, and how a wrong reference bandwidth creates asymmetric paths
svg.desc: Two cost tables side by side. With the default reference bandwidth of one hundred megabits, costs are 1 for a hundred megabit link, 1 for one gigabit, 1 for ten gigabit and 1 for one hundred gigabit, so every link is equal and the metric cannot tell them apart. With a one hundred gigabit reference, the same links cost 1000, 100, 10 and 1, which preserves the real ratio. Below, a topology showing the asymmetry an inconsistent reference bandwidth produces: a ten gigabit link and a one gigabit link between the same two routers, where one router uses the default reference and computes cost 1 for both while the other uses a one hundred gigabit reference and computes 10 and 100, so the forward and return paths differ and troubleshooting traces a path that does not exist in reverse. A closing note gives the design rule: choose the reference so the slowest link in the network is not 1, and set it identically everywhere.
svg.text: Cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth. Above 1 Gbps, the default stops working
The default reference is 100 Mbps, and the result of the division is truncated to an integer — which is where the trouble starts
Every link is equal → the metric is blind
Ratio preserved → the metric means something
WHAT AN INCONSISTENT REFERENCE LOOKS LIKE
10G link · R1 sees cost 1, R2 sees cost 10
1G link · R1 sees cost 1, R2 sees cost 100
Forward and return paths diverge. A traceroute shows a path
that does not exist in reverse — and nobody believes the output.
Choose the reference so that the slowest link in the network
does not come out as 1. If the slowest link is 100 Mbps, a 100 Gbps
reference gives it 1000 and leaves 1000 units of resolution above it.
Then set it identically on every router, and record the value in
the design document — because the value is now part of the topology.
The consequence that shows up in operations: the metric is no longer what you think you configured. Cost is recomputed from the
interface bandwidth by every router locally, so the path is decided by what each router believes its links are — and by the reference
bandwidth it happens to be running. Two routers, two beliefs, one asymmetric network.
Proof to ask for in acceptance: for every link in the topology diagram, print the cost on both ends and compare. A mismatch is not a documentation issue; it is a routing issue.
